title: Swimming Upstream: How One School District is Changing Direction on EdTech
author: Greg Taranto and Mark Abbondanza
summary: In a guest essay for Emily Cherkin's First Fish Chronicles, Pennsylvania's Canon-McMillan superintendent Greg Taranto and colleague Mark Abbondanza describe their district's decision to eliminate Chromebooks in grades K-2 and cut screen time and standalone platforms such as IXL and Reflex Math in grades 3-12. They invest instead in high-quality print materials and cognitive science, with teachers modelling and guiding discussion, because learning depends on sustained attention. They keep a strong technology education program from fifth grade up and argue that technology belongs mainly in dedicated courses. They distinguish traditional ed-tech, which has underperformed teacher-led instruction, from AI, which they say can actively harm learning by removing productive struggle. They cite PISA results and a 2026 JAMA study on screen time, and say vendors influence professional organizations, so they call on more school leaders to swim against the current.
points: The district eliminated Chromebooks in K-2 and is reducing screen time and standalone learning platforms in grades 3-12.
It is investing in high-quality print materials and cognitive science principles, putting the teacher at the center of instruction.
The authors argue AI can harm learning because it removes the productive struggle the brain needs to build understanding.
They cite PISA and a 2026 JAMA study to argue that device dependence correlates with weaker academic outcomes.
They say ed-tech sponsorships shape professional conferences, and urge more leaders to resist the dominant narrative.
quotes: Learning happens through sustained attention, yet big tech companies continue to develop learning platforms that rely on constant switching between tasks to keep students engaged.
The human brain requires productive struggle to build deep understanding. AI is designed to eliminate that struggle by doing the thinking for the user.
If AI handles the thinking, the student does not—and if the student does not think, learning does not occur.
Our stance is that technology belongs primarily in dedicated technology education courses.
Teaching students how technology works is quite different from students sitting in front of a screen.
Because large ed-tech vendors cannot easily monetize these low-cost, research-backed practices, they receive far less visibility in the broader educational market.
We need more school leaders who are willing to swim against ed-tech’s massive current.
